```{r}
# Download R packages
library(tidyverse)
library(openxlsx)
library(patchwork)
library(ggrepel)
library(scales)
library(extrafont)

# Make the Windows fonts available to the plots (Trebuchet MS, as in the text)
loadfonts(device = "win", quiet = TRUE)
```

```{r}
# Spending data: one row per contestant and spending category (amounts in MDL and EUR)
# MM and BUN are left out, as in the previous post
spending_data <- read.xlsx("spending_data_long.xlsx") %>%
  filter(!Competitor_Acronym %in% c("MM", "BUN")) %>%
  # tidy two category labels
  mutate(spending_category_en = case_match(spending_category_en,
                                           "Production/airing comercials" ~ "Broadcast advertisements",
                                           "Premises: rent/maintenance" ~ "Premises",
                                           .default = spending_category_en)) %>%
  group_by(Competitor_Acronym) %>%
  # total = net spending, stack = sum of the positive items
  mutate(total_eur = sum(Amount_EUR),
         total_mdl = sum(amount),
         stack_eur = sum(Amount_EUR[Amount_EUR >= 0])) %>%
  ungroup() %>%
  mutate(Competitor_Acronym = fct_reorder(Competitor_Acronym, total_eur),
         # keep the three largest categories and group the rest
         category = fct_lump_n(spending_category_en, n = 3, w = pmax(Amount_EUR, 0),
                               other_level = "All other categories"),
         category = fct_relevel(category, "All other categories", "Promotional materials",
                                "Broadcast advertisements", "Volunteer activities"))

# One row per contestant with total spending
spending_totals <- spending_data %>%
  distinct(Competitor_Acronym, total_eur, total_mdl, stack_eur)

# Share of each category in the spending of each contestant (rows = contestants)
spending_share <- spending_data %>%
  filter(Amount_EUR >= 0) %>%
  mutate(share = Amount_EUR / sum(Amount_EUR), .by = Competitor_Acronym) %>%
  select(Competitor_Acronym, spending_category_en, share) %>%
  pivot_wider(names_from = spending_category_en, values_from = share) %>%
  column_to_rownames("Competitor_Acronym")

# Amounts in euro by contestant and category (rows = contestants)
spending_eur <- spending_data %>%
  select(Competitor_Acronym, spending_category_en, Amount_EUR) %>%
  pivot_wider(names_from = spending_category_en, values_from = Amount_EUR) %>%
  column_to_rownames("Competitor_Acronym")

# Share of each category in the spending of all contestants
category_share <- spending_data %>%
  filter(Amount_EUR >= 0) %>%
  summarise(eur = sum(Amount_EUR), .by = spending_category_en) %>%
  mutate(share = eur / sum(eur)) %>%
  select(spending_category_en, share) %>%
  deframe()

# Spending cap per contestant (MDL) set by the CEC for the 2025 and 2021 elections
cap_2025 <- 75932486
cap_2021 <- 20707700
spending_totals <- spending_totals %>%
  mutate(cap_share = total_mdl / cap_2025)

# Six best-funded contestants versus all others: share of spending on broadcast advertisements
top6 <- c("BEP", "PAS", "BEA", "PN", "MRM", "AM")
broadcast_others <- spending_share[!rownames(spending_share) %in% top6, "Broadcast advertisements"]
promo_top6 <- spending_share[top6, "Promotional materials"]
```

This is the second post based on my analysis in the Moldovan Analytical Digest [@lipcean2026]. The [first post](../2026-03-15-moldova-2025-campaign-income/index.qmd) looked at how contestants raised money in Moldova's 2025 parliamentary elections. Here I look at the other side: how much they spent, what they spent it on, and whether contestants with a lot of money spent differently from those with little. As before, the analysis uses the official financial reports that contestants filed with the Central Electoral Commission (CEC) [@cec2025financial], and therefore covers only declared spending. The figures cover the same `r nrow(spending_totals)` contestants as in the previous post.

::: {.callout-note collapse="true"}
## Acronyms of electoral contestants

```{r}
read.xlsx("acronims.xlsx") %>%
  rename(Acronym = party_acronym, `Electoral contestant` = party_name_en) %>%
  knitr::kable()
```
:::

***How much did contestants spend?***

The law capped each contestant's spending at 0.1% of state budget revenues: MDL 75,932,486, or about €3.9 million [@cec2025cap]. That is roughly MDL 28 (€1.4) per registered voter. In the 2021 elections the cap was half as large as a share of the budget (0.05%, or MDL 20,707,700 [@cec2021cap]), so the 2025 cap was about `r round(cap_2025 / cap_2021, 1)` times higher in lei. In practice, nobody came close to it. The biggest spender, the Patriotic Electoral Bloc (BEP), used `r percent(max(spending_totals$cap_share), accuracy = 1)` of the cap, and the Party of Action and Solidarity (PAS), the party in government, `r percent(spending_totals$cap_share[spending_totals$Competitor_Acronym == "PAS"], accuracy = 1)`. Most contestants spent less than 2%.

Together, electoral competitors reported about `r dollar(sum(spending_totals$total_eur) / 1e6, prefix = "€", accuracy = 0.1, suffix = " million")` in campaign spending. Given the interchangeability of income and spending totals, reported spending matches reported income almost to the euro (the largest difference is about €10), so the ranking is the same as for income. The inequality in fundraising described in the previous post is therefore also an inequality in spending. The interesting question is how contestants allocated their campaign money for different purposes to win the voters' hearts and endorsement.

***Where did the money go?***

@fig-spending breaks spending down into four broad categories. Panel A ranks contestants based on spending budgets from the largest to the smallest. It also shows the distribution of spending categories in absolute numbers. Panel B displays the distribution of spending categories in percentage, which provides a more nuanced perspective on how contestants prioritised the allocation of campaign money for different purposes. To keep the figure readable, I show the three largest categories separately and lump all the others together. The three categories that dominate spending priorities include: volunteer activities (`r percent(category_share[["Volunteer activities"]], accuracy = 1)` of all reported spending), broadcast advertisements (`r percent(category_share[["Broadcast advertisements"]], accuracy = 1)`) and promotional materials (`r percent(category_share[["Promotional materials"]], accuracy = 1)`). Together they account for `r percent(category_share[["Volunteer activities"]] + category_share[["Broadcast advertisements"]] + category_share[["Promotional materials"]], accuracy = 1)` of all campaign spending. The remaining categories are insignificant: in-kind goods and services account for `r percent(category_share[["In-kind: goods/services"]], accuracy = 1)`, transport for `r percent(category_share[["Transport"]], accuracy = 1)`, while premises, personnel and legal fees are each below 0.5%.

```{r}
#| label: fig-spending
#| fig-cap: "Campaign spending of electoral contestants in Moldova's 2025 parliamentary elections, by spending category. Panel A shows absolute amounts (the label is the net total spending), panel B the share of each category. The three largest categories are shown separately, all others are grouped."
#| fig-alt: "Two stacked bar charts of campaign spending by contestant. Panel A shows absolute amounts in thousand euro, with BEP and PAS above 1.2 million and most contestants below 100 thousand. Panel B shows the share of volunteer activities, broadcast advertisements, promotional materials and all other categories."
#| fig-height: 4.5
#| fig-width: 8

# Panel A: absolute amounts
absolute_sp <- spending_data %>%
  filter(Amount_EUR >= 0) %>%
  ggplot(aes(x = Competitor_Acronym,
             y = Amount_EUR / 1000,
             fill = fct_rev(category))) +
  geom_col() +
  geom_text(data = spending_totals,
            aes(x = Competitor_Acronym,
                y = stack_eur / 1000,
                label = comma(total_eur / 1000, accuracy = 1)),
            inherit.aes = FALSE, hjust = -0.1, size = 3, family = "Trebuchet MS") +
  scale_y_continuous(breaks = seq(0, 1500, 300),
                     labels = comma,
                     expand = expansion(mult = c(0, 0.12))) +
  scale_fill_viridis_d(name = "Spending categories", end = 0.9) +
  guides(fill = guide_legend(reverse = TRUE)) +
  coord_flip() +
  theme_light(base_family = "Trebuchet MS") +
  theme(
    panel.grid.minor = element_blank(),
    panel.grid.major = element_line(linetype = 3),
    legend.background = element_rect(fill = "transparent"),
    plot.title = element_text(size = 12),
    legend.key.height = unit(0.8, "lines"),
    legend.key.width = unit(0.8, "lines"),
    legend.position = "inside",
    legend.position.inside = c(0.65, 0.25)
  ) +
  labs(title = "A: Absolute numbers", x = "", y = "€ thousand")

# Panel B: share of each category in the spending of each contestant
relative_sp <- spending_data %>%
  filter(Amount_EUR >= 0) %>%
  ggplot(aes(x = Competitor_Acronym,
             y = Amount_EUR,
             fill = fct_rev(category))) +
  geom_col(position = position_fill()) +
  scale_y_continuous(labels = percent) +
  scale_fill_viridis_d(name = "Spending categories", end = 0.9) +
  coord_flip() +
  theme_light(base_family = "Trebuchet MS") +
  theme(
    axis.text.y = element_blank(),
    plot.title = element_text(size = 12),
    panel.grid.minor = element_blank(),
    panel.grid.major = element_line(linetype = 3),
    legend.position = "none"
  ) +
  labs(title = "B: Percentage", x = "", y = "Percentage")

# Combine both panels
absolute_sp + relative_sp
```

***Volunteers***

Volunteer work represents the largest spending item and is reported on both sides of the campaign budget, as income (what supporters contribute) and as spending (the value of their work, as reported by the contestant). This is also the category where the gap between electoral contestants is widest. For BEP, volunteer activities make up `r percent(spending_share["BEP", "Volunteer activities"], accuracy = 1)` of reported spending, and for the Respect Moldova Movement (MRM) `r percent(spending_share["MRM", "Volunteer activities"], accuracy = 1)`. For PAS, the party in government, it accounts for `r percent(spending_share["PAS", "Volunteer activities"], accuracy = 1)` of expenses. The majority of smaller contestants report little or no volunteer activity at all. We know that the ability to mobilize volunteers is a sign of relatively strong organisation.

What type of work did volunteers carry out? In the digest I used the detailed campaign reports of each contestant to show that about three quarters of volunteer activities, around 30,000 in all, consisted in handing out campaign materials in direct contact with voters. More than 6,000 worked as representatives at polling stations, and the rest helped with media, logistics and other support [@lipcean2026].

***Broadcast advertisements and promotional materials***

Broadcast advertisements are the second biggest item, and here the picture is different. PAS spent `r dollar(spending_eur["PAS", "Broadcast advertisements"], prefix = "€", accuracy = 1)` on producing and airing commercials, `r percent(spending_share["PAS", "Broadcast advertisements"], accuracy = 1)` of its spending, more than any other contestant in euros. The other big spenders had other priorities: BEP devoted only `r percent(spending_share["BEP", "Broadcast advertisements"], accuracy = 1)` of its spending to commercials, BEA `r percent(spending_share["BEA", "Broadcast advertisements"], accuracy = 1)` and PN `r percent(spending_share["PN", "Broadcast advertisements"], accuracy = 1)`. Among the less well-funded contestants, commercials were typically a *larger* share of the budget than for their wealthier counterparts. Outside the six best-funded contestants, the typical share spent on broadcast advertisements revolves around `r percent(median(broadcast_others), accuracy = 1)`, although several of them spent on broadcasting ads more than two thirds of their entire budget. Paid commercials were regarded by electoral competitors with little resources and limited organisation capacity to get campaign visibility to offset the shortage of a volunteer network.

Promotional materials, such as printed leaflets and posters, constitute the third spending category. Across the six best-funded contestants, they account for between `r percent(min(promo_top6), accuracy = 1)` and `r percent(max(promo_top6), accuracy = 1)` of spending, which suggests that such outlays are a routine cost for contestants with an established organisational structure.

@fig-strategies displays the share of campaign spending for each of the two dominant categories -- broadcasting ads and volunteer work -- against each other. Each point is a contestant, located by the share of its spending for volunteer activities (horizontal axis) and to broadcast advertisements (vertical axis), while the size and colour of each point show how much the respective contestant spent in total. As the plot shows, contestants spread along a diagonal, from campaigns investing almost exclusively in advertisements (upper left) to campaigns prioritizing volunteer work (lower right). The well-funded competitors and big spenders are scattered in different places: BEP and MRM relied mostly on volunteers, PAS and BEA are in the middle, while most poorly funded contestants are located in the top left corner.

```{r}
#| label: fig-strategies
#| fig-cap: "Campaign spending strategies of electoral contestants in Moldova's 2025 parliamentary elections: share of spending on volunteer activities and on broadcast advertisements. The size of the point shows total spending."
#| fig-alt: "A scatter plot where each point is a contestant. The horizontal axis shows the share of spending on volunteer activities, the vertical axis the share on broadcast advertisements. Point size shows total spending. BEP is at the far right, many small contestants are in the upper left."
#| fig-height: 4
#| fig-width: 7

spending_share %>%
  rownames_to_column("Competitor_Acronym") %>%
  left_join(spending_totals, by = "Competitor_Acronym") %>%
  ggplot(aes(x = `Volunteer activities`,
             y = `Broadcast advertisements`,
             size = total_eur / 1000,
             colour = total_eur / 1000)) +
  geom_point(alpha = 0.8) +
  geom_text_repel(aes(label = Competitor_Acronym), colour = "grey30", size = 3, family = "Trebuchet MS") +
  scale_x_continuous(labels = percent) +
  scale_y_continuous(labels = percent) +
  scale_size_continuous(name = "Total spending\n€ thousand",
                        breaks = c(10, 50, 250, 500, 1000, 1500),
                        labels = comma,
                        range = c(1, 10)) +
  scale_colour_viridis_c(name = "Total spending\n€ thousand",
                         breaks = c(10, 50, 250, 500, 1000, 1500),
                         labels = comma,
                         end = 0.9) +
  guides(size = guide_legend(), colour = guide_legend()) + # merge both legends
  labs(x = "Share of spending on volunteer activities",
       y = "Share of spending on broadcast advertisements") +
  theme_light(base_family = "Trebuchet MS") +
  theme(panel.grid.minor = element_blank(),
        panel.grid.major = element_line(linetype = 3))
```

***What this means for competition***

Given that campaign spending represents the flip side of fundraising, it reflects the same disparities in resources: several contestants spent considerably more than most of other competitors. The top-tier spenders had more options regarding how to allocate their funds between different categories. However, as data show, they had different preferences on how to combine volunteer work, media coverage and organisation. In contrast, contestants with limited funds had a much narrower choice. Without an extensive organisation and a narrow volunteer pool, they channeled most of their money into paid commercials to increase visibility.

These resource disparities raise a critical question: do they ultimately translate into votes? I provide a tentative answer in the next post.
